summary: A changing network of colonies, trading posts and maritime routes spanning Africa, Asia and the Americas under Portuguese rule.
capital: Lisbon for most of the period; Rio de Janeiro replaced it as the imperial capital in 1808–1821.
currency: Real in metropolitan Portugal, replaced by the escudo in 1911; colonial currencies differed by territory.
economy: Maritime commerce, African gold, plantation production and the slave trade supported imperial connections; slavery was central to Portuguese America.
military: Fortified trading posts and overseas conquests supported maritime expansion; military capacity and control varied sharply between territories.
contributions: Oceanic routes linked previously separate trading systems and generated lasting cultural exchanges alongside slavery and colonial violence.
origin: The conquest of Ceuta in 1415 preceded Atlantic expansion and the establishment of overseas settlements and trading posts.
decline: Decolonization accelerated after the 1974 revolution; Portugal recognized African colonial independence in 1974–1975 and ended its administration of Macao in 1999.
periodNote: 1415 marks Ceuta’s conquest; 1999 marks the Macao handover. This umbrella record spans different regimes and does not imply uniformly controlled territory.
